newsitem.title: USA: Sprint to buy Paranet for $425 million.
newsitem.headline: Sprint to buy Paranet for $425 million.

text.p: Sprint Corp., aiming to expand into the lucrative computer network systems management business, said Monday it agreed to buy Paranet Inc. for $425 million in cash.

Called "Sprint Paranet," the new business unit will provide systems management services, including the design and day-to-day management of computer networks, intranets and use of the Internet. Intranets are private computer networks that operate using the Internet's technical standards.

"Many businesses are asking Sprint to help them simplify the design and management of their network systems," said Sprint Chairman William Esrey. "Sprint Paranet gives our customers much needed access to high-quality, proven services that help fully exploit the competitive advantage of properly utilized network assets."
Esrey said the addition of Paranet extends Sprint's services to the desktop and allows the company to provide end-to-end network services.

Sprint already provides companies with networks of long-distance lines, or WANs (wide area networks) which connect, for example, a company's various offices. The acquisition of Paranet will also allow them to set up and manage complex LANs (local area networks), which connect personal computers within a building.

"By having this capability available to the high-end business markets, it not only allows Sprint to attract more customers but helps to keep them," said Tony Ferrugia, the telecommunications analyst for investment bankers A.G. Edwards & Sons. "It's a positive step."
Westwood, Kan.-based Sprint said the acquisition will not affect its 1997 earnings, and in 1998 Sprint Paranet is expected to report a profit. The deal is expected to close by the end of 1997.

Sprint said nearly 50 percent of all businesses already outsource some or all of their network and system management needs. The U.S. market for network management services is currently worth about $27 billion and is expected to grow to about $43 billion by the year 2000, it said.

"This is not just a technology issue, but an integration of hardware, software, networks and people, which produces the highly productive environments that give companies a competitive edge," said Michael Holthouse, president and founder of Houston-based Paranet.
Holthouse has been appointed president of Sprint Paranet.

In acquiring Paranet, Sprint will come up against the same competitors it faces in the long-distance telephone market, MCI Communications Corp. and AT&T Corp. T.N.. In 1995, MCI acquired SHL Systemhouse for $1 billion in stock and formed MCI Systemhouse. AT&T Corp has its AT&T Solutions unit, targeting a similar market.

As part of Sprint, the Sprint Paranet unit will design and deliver networks using networking, system and computer components from throughout the industry. This will allow Sprint Paranet customers to continue to use their existing equipment while changing to new and more effective technology, the company said.
With 1,100 employees, Paranet serves more than 250 major customers. Paranet recorded 1996 revenues of $66 million, and revenues are expected to be approximately double in 1997, Sprint said.
Sprint has $14 billion in annual revenues and serves more than 16 million business and residential customers.
Sprint traded down 44 cents a share at $45.125 in composite trading on the New York Stock Exchange Monday afternoon.
